428.title: Block A close: the long surahs
428.hook: law, story, battle and mercy woven together, and every surah but one opening with mercy
428.howItsDone: Muslims begin the recitation of every surah except at-Tawbah with bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim, and many who read the Qur'an through mark the end of the long opening surahs as a milestone in their reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last verse of at-Tawbah: even if they turn away, hasbiya Allah, God is enough for me. Your line was allah is enough. When a worry tightened, did the line come first? Day four hundred twenty-eight, the last day of Block A.

Ninety-five days ago, this year began with seven verses said seventeen times a day. Since then we've walked through the long surahs at the front of the Qur'an, most of them revealed in Medina, where a small community became a city with neighbors, treaties, marriages, markets and wars. A reader expecting a holy book of nothing but prayer finds something else here. Inheritance shares sit beside the Throne verse. A debt contract sits beside a prayer for strength. A battle sits beside a verse about a single heart. It's all woven together. And nearly every one of those surahs opens the same way.

Here's Block A in nine doors. Al-Fatiha: a conversation, praise and then asking. Al-Baqarah: the cow, the Throne verse, no compulsion in religion, write your debts down, and a God who burdens no soul beyond what it can bear. Al 'Imran: Maryam, chosen above the women of the worlds, a common word with the People of the Book, and the Prophet's gentleness: had you been harsh, they would have scattered. An-Nisa: live with them in kindness, stand for justice even against yourselves, greet with something better. Al-Ma'idah: whoever saves one life, it is as if he saved all humanity; compete in good; the table from heaven. Al-An'am: not a leaf falls without His knowing; don't insult the gods of others. Al-A'raf: am I not your Lord, asked before we were born, and the garment of piety. Al-Anfal: if they incline to peace, incline to it too. At-Tawbah: the cave, the three left behind, and enough for me. Law, story, battle, and running through all of it, mercy. Now count the openings. Of the Qur'an's one hundred fourteen surahs, every one opens with bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim, in the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Kind, except at-Tawbah. And, as we saw a week ago, the missing bismillah turns up inside another surah, an-Naml, in a letter from Sulayman, so the phrase still appears one hundred fourteen times. Before every law, every story, every battle in these pages, the reader passes through those words first. However hard the room, mercy was the door you came in by.
screen: `A CONVERSATION; THE THRONE VERSE.` · `MARYAM; JUSTICE; ONE LIFE.` · `NOT A LEAF; AM I NOT YOUR LORD?` · `PEACE; THE CAVE; ENOUGH FOR ME.` · then, large: `MERCY WAS ALWAYS THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one lesson from each of the long surahs. Sit, and breathe. Let the nine doors pass by slowly, one per breath or two: the Fatiha, the Cow, the Family of 'Imran, the Women, the Table, the Cattle, the Heights, the Spoils, the Repentance. At each one, let a single line or picture come back, whatever stayed with you. Don't force it. When the bell ends, write them down, nine short lines. If you pray, you can begin with bismillah. The bell holds the time.
Bismillah, in the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Kind. The door that opens every surah but one, appearing one hundred fourteen times in all. Today's word.
Your line: mercy was always the door. Tomorrow Block B begins: prophets, parables and light, starting with Surah Yunus. Today, read your nine lines once, and keep them. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

429.title: The friends of Allah
429.hook: no fear on them nor grief: those who believe and are mindful (10:62–63)
429.howItsDone: Muslims recite 10:62–64 as a comfort and as a description of God's friends; in many places the word wali is also used for revered saints whose tombs people visit, a practice some Muslims embrace and others discourage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bismillah, the Block A close, the long surahs from al-Baqarah to at-Tawbah, and your line was mercy was always the door. Which of those surahs stayed with you? Day four hundred twenty-nine, and a new block begins.

Block B: prophets, parables and light. We leave the long surahs revealed in Medina and step into a run of surahs usually placed in Mecca, named for prophets: Yunus, Hud, Yusuf, Ibrahim. Surah ten carries Yunus's name, though he appears in it only once, near the end. Before we get there, the surah answers a question people in every age have asked about holy people. Who are the friends of God? A few saints in a painting? A hermit on a mountain? Verse sixty-two gives a word for them, and verse sixty-three gives a definition that surprises people.

Pickthall's translation of verse sixty-two: "Lo! verily the friends of Allah are (those) on whom fear (cometh) not, nor do they grieve." The word is awliya', friends, the plural of wali, from the same root we met in at-Tawbah, the one that means to be near. Last week it ran between believers. Here it runs between people and God. Then the next verse defines them, in paraphrase: those who believe and keep mindful of God. That's all. Believe, and have taqwa. No miracles required, no famous name. Over the centuries the word wali also came to mean a saint, especially in Sufi tradition, where great teachers are called awliya' and their tombs are visited. Some Muslims honor those figures; others, especially in reformist movements, are wary of the practices around tombs. Both sides read the same verse, and both point to the same definition. Now the promise: no fear, no grief. Some commentators split the two this way: fear looks forward, at what might happen; grief looks back, at what already did. The friends of God are spared both, at least in the deepest sense. And a hadith qudsi in Bukhari describes how someone draws near. God says, in paraphrase: My servant comes close to Me through what I've made obligatory, and keeps coming closer through extra acts of devotion, until I love him. And when I love him, I become the hearing he hears with, the sight he sees with. The friendship is not a rank you're born into. It's a nearness you walk into, one ordinary act at a time.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one fear go. Sit, and breathe. Notice where fear lives in you right now, the forward-looking worry about something that hasn't happened. Name it, quietly. Then notice if there's a grief too, something from behind you. You don't have to solve either one. For these two minutes, set the fear down in front of you and the grief behind you, and just sit in the middle, here. If you pray, you can recite the verse, or simply say: Ya Wali. The bell holds the time.
Wali. A friend, an ally, someone near; plural awliya'. The friends of God are those who believe and are mindful. Today's word.
Your line: no fear, no grief. Today, when a worry about tomorrow comes up, ask: is this fear, looking ahead, or grief, looking back? Day four hundred twenty-nine.

430.title: Too late
430.hook: Pharaoh believes as he drowns, and his body is kept as a sign (10:90–92)
430.howItsDone: Muslim teachers use Pharaoh's last words in 10:90–92 to teach that repentance should come while there is still a choice, alongside the hadith that God accepts repentance until the death rattle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wali, the friends of God, who believe and are mindful. Your line was no fear, no grief. When a worry came, was it fear looking ahead, or grief looking back? Day four hundred thirty.

The sea has opened, and a people who were slaves in Egypt are walking through it on dry ground. Behind them, chariots. Pharaoh and his army have chased them to the water's edge and, with the whole might of Egypt behind them, ridden straight in after them. The Qur'an tells this crossing in several surahs. Surah Yunus stops on a single moment: the water closing over Pharaoh's head, and Pharaoh finally saying the words Musa had been asking him to say.

Verse ninety, in paraphrase: when drowning overtook him, Pharaoh said, I believe that there is no god but the one the Children of Israel believe in, and I am of those who submit. Notice the words. I am of the muslimin, those who submit. It's the right sentence. It's almost a creed. And the answer comes in verse ninety-one: Now? When you rebelled before, and were among the corrupters? It's not that the words were wrong. It's when they came. Again and again Musa brought signs: a staff, a hand, a flood, locusts, frogs, blood. Each time Pharaoh promised, and each time he went back. Only with water in his throat did he say it, and by then it wasn't a choice anymore, only a sight he couldn't deny. A hadith reported by at-Tirmidhi says God accepts a servant's repentance until the death rattle reaches the throat. The door stays open a long time. But not forever. Then verse ninety-two, in Pickthall's translation: "But this day We save thee in thy body that thou mayst be a portent for those after thee." His body is kept, a sign for whoever comes later. Which Pharaoh was it? The Qur'an doesn't say, and neither does the Bible's telling in Exodus. Some modern writers link the verse to preserved royal bodies in Egyptian museums; historians have not settled who the Pharaoh of the exodus was, or whether one can be named at all. What the verse keeps is the timing. The right words, too late, become a warning rather than a rescue.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't delay one right thing. Sit, and breathe. Think of a right thing you've been putting off. An apology. A phone call to someone getting old. A debt. A visit. Something you know you'll do, someday. Picture it clearly. Then picture doing it today, in its smallest possible version: a text that starts the apology, a date in the calendar for the visit. If you pray, you can ask for help not to wait. The bell holds the time.
Too late. Pharaoh says the right words only as the sea closes over him, and the answer comes: now? Today's word.
Your line: don't wait for the water. Today, do the smallest version of the thing you pictured, before the day is over. Day four hundred thirty.

431.title: The town that turned
431.hook: only the people of Yunus turned back in time and were spared (10:98)
431.howItsDone: Muslim preachers often tell the story of the people of Yunus when calling a community to repentance, as the Qur'an's example of a whole town that turned back in time and was spared.

segments.voice: Yesterday, too late: Pharaoh's right words as the sea closed. Your line was don't wait for the water. Did you do the smallest version of the thing you'd been putting off? Day four hundred thirty-one.

Read the Qur'an's stories of earlier peoples in a row and a pattern shows up. A prophet comes. He warns. The people mock him. The warning comes true. Nuh's people, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lut, Pharaoh. Again and again, the same ending. So when yesterday's story ends with Pharaoh in the water, you might expect the next one to end the same way. Then, a few verses later, Surah Yunus stops and asks a question: why was there no town that believed in time? And it gives one exception. Just one. The town that gives the surah its name.

Verse ninety-eight, in paraphrase: if only there had been a town that believed, and its belief had benefited it, except the people of Yunus. When they believed, God lifted from them the punishment of disgrace in this life, and let them enjoy life for a while. The Qur'an doesn't name the town; many commentators say Nineveh, on the Tigris, the same city named in the Bible's book of Jonah, which Jews and Christians read too. Here's the strange part. In the account many commentators give, Yunus wasn't there for it. Other surahs tell how he went off in anger, fled to a laden ship, and was swallowed by the great fish. The commentators place the town's turning behind him: the people saw the first signs of the punishment, and they went out of the city together, men, women and children, and cried out to God, and turned. And the punishment that was coming was lifted. So in the very surah that holds Pharaoh's too late, there is a whole city that was not too late. The door that closes at the death rattle was still wide open for them, and they walked through it at the last moment, all at once. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once said, in a hadith in Bukhari: don't say I'm better than Yunus son of Matta. The prophet who went off in anger is honored by name, and so is the town that turned behind his back. One verse, and it changes how you hear all the stories around it. The pattern isn't fate. It can break.

Now picture turning, right there, in some small way. If you pray, you can ask God to turn toward you, the way He turned toward the town. The bell holds the time.
Yunus. The prophet whose people, after seeing the first signs of punishment, turned back and were spared, the one exception named in Surah Yunus. Today's word.
Your line: it's not too late. Today, catch one old pattern just before it starts, and turn it, even by a degree. Day four hundred thirty-one.

432.title: Would you compel them?
432.hook: had your Lord willed, all would believe, so would you compel people (10:99)
432.tomorrow: The surah that turned him gray
432.howItsDone: Muslim scholars cite 10:99 alongside 2:256, 'there is no compulsion in religion,' when teaching that faith must be freely chosen and that a believer's task is to convey the message, not to force it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yunus, the people who turned back, the one town that believed in time. Your line was it's not too late. Which old pattern did you catch and turn? Day four hundred thirty-two.

A parent and a grown child at the same table, seeing the world two different ways. Or two old friends. One of them is sure, and can see exactly how much easier the other's life would be with a little agreement. So comes the push. One more article. One more argument at dinner. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ felt that pull about his own people in Mecca: his neighbors, his relatives, the clan he grew up in. The Qur'an says elsewhere he nearly wore himself out with grief over them. And right after yesterday's town, Surah Yunus asks him a question.

Verse ninety-nine, in Pickthall's translation: "And if thy Lord willed, all who are in the earth would have believed together. Wouldst thou (Muhammad) compel men until they are believers?" Read the first half slowly. If God wanted a world where everyone believed, He could have had one. He didn't make that world. He made a world where people choose. And then the question, aimed at the messenger, who had every reason to push: would you compel them? The Arabic verb is tukrihu, from the root k-r-h, to force someone into what they dislike. The same root gives a line from al-Baqarah, which Pickthall renders: "There is no compulsion in religion." The next verse, one hundred, adds that no soul believes except by God's leave. Belief is not something one person can install in another. Commentators read verse ninety-nine as comfort as much as instruction. The Prophet's task was to convey the message clearly. What people did with it was between them and God. That lifted a weight he couldn't have carried anyway. Scholars across the centuries have discussed how this principle sits beside the Qur'an's verses about war and law, and they've debated the details. But the question in this verse is still asked plainly, and it's addressed to the Prophet himself. If the one who brought the message wasn't to force it, the line runs through everyone who loves someone and disagrees with them.

If you pray, you can pray for them, and leave the rest with God. The bell holds the time.

Your line: not by force. Today, in one disagreement with someone you love, say your view once, clearly, and then stop. Day four hundred thirty-two.

433.title: The surah that turned him gray
433.hook: the Prophet ﷺ said Hud and its sisters had turned his hair gray (Tirmidhi)
433.howItsDone: Teachers of Qur'an recitation often cite the hadith 'Hud and its sisters turned me gray' to encourage slow, attentive recitation, and some Muslims read Surah Hud with special seriousness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last day in Surah Yunus, and its question about compulsion: would you compel them? Your line was not by force. Did you say your view once, and stop? Day four hundred thirty-three.

Abu Bakr looked at his friend one day and noticed something. A few white hairs in the beard. Not many. Anas, who served the Prophet for years, said later that at the end of his life there weren't even twenty white hairs on his head and beard together. But Abu Bakr saw them, and said so: Messenger of God, you've gone gray. The answer he got is the reason we start Surah Hud this way. Not with a story, though Hud is full of stories. With a confession of how heavy these words were to carry.

At-Tirmidhi records the answer. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: Hud turned me gray, and al-Waqi'ah, and al-Mursalat, and 'Amma yatasa'alun, and Idha ash-shamsu kuwwirat. Hud and its sisters. Look at what they share. The four sisters are shorter surahs, in the later part of the Qur'an, about the Day the sun is folded up, the stars fall and every soul sees what it did. Hud is long, the eleventh surah, and it tells, one after another, the stories of prophets and their peoples: Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, Shu'ayb, Musa. Ending after ending. Scholars have asked: what exactly in Hud weighed on him? One answer, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, points to a single verse, one hundred twelve: so stand firm, as you have been commanded, you and those who turn with you, and don't overstep. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have said that no verse was harder on the Prophet than that one. It's not a threat. It's a command to keep going straight, every day, without drifting, and to carry others with you. Elsewhere the Qur'an tells him it will lay on him a weighty word. These surahs are weighty words. Some readers find this hadith a comfort. The Prophet didn't read the Qur'an lightly. He felt it in his body, down to a few white hairs.

If you pray, you can sit with the verse in Arabic or in your own language. The bell holds the time.
Hud. The surah that the Prophet said, with its sisters, had turned his hair gray. Today's word.
Your line: weighty words. Today, read one line of anything you take seriously, a verse, a letter, a vow, twice as slowly as you usually would. Day four hundred thirty-three.

434.title: The ark in full
434.hook: Nuh builds, the waters come, and the ark sails in Allah's name (11:37–41)
434.carry: in his name it sails and anchors
434.howItsDone: Some Muslims recite Nuh's words from 11:41, bismillahi majraha wa mursaha, when boarding a ship or setting out on a journey, alongside the traveler's supplication taught in the hadith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hud, the surah that turned him gray, and your line was weighty words. Which line did you read twice as slowly? Day four hundred thirty-four, the end of a week.

This week opened Block B. We met the friends of God, with no fear and no grief. We watched Pharaoh say the right words too late, and a whole town say them just in time. We heard the question, would you compel them, and learned why Hud turned the Prophet's hair gray. Now Hud's first long story. Last year you watched Nuh build on dry land while the neighbors laughed, and call to his son on the mountain. Today we take the voyage itself, start to finish, because Surah Hud gives it a shape, and a single line people still say when they set out.
screen: `A WEEK: FEAR, TOO LATE, IN TIME.`

segments.voice: It begins with a command, in verse thirty-seven: build the ship under Our eyes and by Our inspiration. Bi-a'yunina: under Our eyes. Every plank laid while being watched over. Then the sign comes, water gushing out, and the order: load on it a pair of every kind, your household, and those who believe. And the verse adds, almost quietly: and they were only a few. Then Nuh speaks, in Pickthall's translation: "Embark therein! In the name of Allah be its course and its mooring." Bismillahi majraha wa mursaha. Majra is the sailing, the running of the ship; mursa is the anchoring, the coming to rest. Both in God's name: the going and the stopping. Some Muslims still say these words when they board a boat or set out on a journey. The middle of the voyage is the hard part: waves like mountains, and the son who would not come aboard, whom you met last year. Then the ending, in verse forty-four, in a run of short commands. Earth, swallow your water. Sky, hold back. The water sinks away, the command is fulfilled, the ship comes to rest on al-Judi. And in verse forty-eight, the last word to Nuh: go down, in peace from Us, and with blessings on you and on the peoples who will come from those with you. Read in full, the voyage has three parts. It sets out in God's name. It comes to rest in God's name. And it steps off in peace.
screen: `BUILD IT UNDER OUR EYES.` · `AND THEY WERE ONLY A FEW.` · `IN GOD'S NAME, ITS COURSE AND MOORING.` · `EARTH, SWALLOW; SKY, HOLD BACK.` · then, large: `IN HIS NAME IT SAILS AND ANCHORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin a journey with bismillah. Sit, and breathe. Think of the next journey you'll take, even a small one: the drive to work, the walk to the store, the flight next month. Picture the moment you set off, and the moment you arrive. If you pray, you can say Nuh's words at both ends: in God's name its course, in God's name its mooring. If not, simply give the start and the stop a breath of attention. The bell holds the time.
Al-Judi. The mountain where Nuh's ark came to rest, after God's command: earth, swallow your water; sky, hold back. Today's word.
Your line: in his name it sails and anchors. Today, mark the start and the end of one trip with a breath, or with bismillah. Day four hundred thirty-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: animals two by two.
what it means: a voyage that sets out in God's name, rests in God's name, and ends in peace.
what a scholar hears: majra and mursa are read as both place and time of sailing and anchoring; 11:44 is studied by rhetoricians for its compressed commands to earth and sky.
